The draft is safe. It refers Johnny to a physio this week for an Achilles that got sharper with pace. It drops all faster running, gives a clear stop rule (above 3/10 or a change in stride) and cuts volume to about 21–23 mi, plus cross-training in place of a run. The long run drops to 8–10 mi. The fixed Monday and Friday rest days are kept, and every day can be run as written with pace and heart-rate limits. That suits a cautious runner with a history of shin splints and a race close ahead.

The big weakness is that it doesn't really answer either question. Both replies pass the question to a clinician ("I can't make that call", "that is a clinician's job"). Yet the plan does make the call: keep going with easy runs. The draft could also have given Johnny simple warning signs to watch for, such as swelling, pain when hopping, morning stiffness that gets worse, or pain that gets worse during a run. An anxious athlete asking two direct questions gets two deflections. Answering the athlete is one of the most important qualities, so the draft can't score higher than average.
